title: Tesla gave up the EV crown. Now it wants to win the autonomy race.
gist: Per the FT, Tesla ceded the EV crown to BYD and Musk is now betting on autonomy and software, with the Roadster stunt followed days later by word that SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger. Analysts see Full Self-Driving, with 1.7 million subscriptions, as the margin engine, while regulatory approval, Chinese rivals such as Xpeng and merger risks remain.

insights.claim: Carmakers, already facing growing Chinese competition, are trying to shift from a business model centered on vehicle sales to one that also generates recurring revenue from software and AI-powered services.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Valuation multiples of autos will increasingly depend on software mix rather than unit volume.
insights.quote: seeking to move beyond a business model centered on vehicle sales

insights.claim: Dan Ives says automakers see software as the golden goose because the margins are so high.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Industry-wide pursuit of software margins raises competition and pricing pressure.
insights.quote: the software piece is what they are all looking at as the golden goose, because the margins are so high

insights.claim: Autonomous driving has become a major battleground for the global car industry as EVs with similar ranges and pricing proliferate, so competition is shifting from hardware to autonomy.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: As EV hardware commoditizes, autonomy is the differentiator.
insights.quote: Autonomous driving in particular has become a major battleground
insights.locator: Whether or not the companies merge

insights.claim: Autobrains' CEO says leading carmakers are reconsidering strategy completely and want a subscription model with more advanced eyes-off technology to generate new revenue.
insights.speaker: Igal Raichelgauz
insights.so_what: Expect legacy OEMs to push subscription autonomy tiers.
insights.quote: are trying to reconsider their strategy completely

insights.claim: Tesla's car business generates 75 percent of total revenue, so it stays a cash cow that has to fund the heavy AI spending needed to compete with Big Tech.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Tesla's AI ambitions are funded by a still hardware-dependent business.
insights.quote: it generates 75 percent of total revenues

insights.claim: Musk's goal of 20 million vehicles a year by 2030 has been cut to 5 million, which is still ambitious as Tesla delivered 1.6 million last year.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Unit growth targets have been reset sharply lower, which puts more weight on non-unit revenue.
insights.quote: has been watered down to 5 million

insights.claim: Tesla ceded the title of largest EV maker to BYD last year, and Chinese rivals are now winning the EV race while investing heavily in software and AI.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Tesla's moat is shifting from EV scale to autonomy.
insights.quote: Chinese rivals are now winning the electric vehicle race
insights.locator: But Musk faces a vastly different

insights.claim: Tesla reported its largest car order backlog in four years, with more than 75 percent of new North American Teslas sold with supervised FSD and 1.7 million active FSD subscriptions globally, up 67 percent year over year. Musk claims there is really no competitor for FSD in any car you can buy.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Strong FSD attach and subscription growth support the recurring-revenue thesis.
insights.quote: there’s really no competitor for FSD in any car that you can buy

insights.claim: Tesla has not disclosed how much recurring revenue FSD generates, though it costs $99 a month in the US and priced differently by market.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Investors are valuing the FSD story without disclosed revenue.
insights.quote: has not disclosed how much recurring revenue is generated by FSD

insights.claim: Ives says FSD is already Tesla's highest-margin segment, and expanding it from roughly 10-15 percent of the customer base to about 50 percent would transform the financial model and contribute more than selling an extra 50,000-100,000 cars a year.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Attach-rate expansion is the key lever for Tesla's earnings, more than volume.
insights.quote: transform the whole financial model

insights.claim: Ives argues the market rewards each dollar of FSD revenue 50-70 percent more than a dollar from selling a car.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Mix shift to software would lift the valuation multiple, not just profits.
insights.quote: For every dollar of FSD revenue, the market rewards it 50-70 percent more

insights.claim: Analysts said the near-term key to growth toward 5 million sales is FSD, which despite its name still requires humans in the driver's seat to pay full attention.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The growth narrative rests on software that is not yet autonomous.
insights.quote: still requires humans to sit in the driver’s seat and pay full attention

insights.claim: Tesla has yet to win any approval for its fully autonomous version of FSD, and realizing the FSD potential depends on overcoming regulatory hurdles in multiple markets.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Regulation is the gating item for the upside case.
insights.quote: Tesla has yet to win any approval

insights.claim: Tesla's supervised FSD is approved in the Netherlands and several other European countries, but an EU-wide rollout needs a member-state vote that has been delayed until December.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The December vote is a near-term catalyst for the European FSD story.
insights.quote: a vote of member states that has been delayed until December

insights.claim: Xpeng is working with German authorities and targets EU approval for its XNGP system after the bloc adopts regulations expected early next year, and its general counsel says it aims to be one of the first.
insights.speaker: Zheng Yeqing
insights.so_what: Chinese rivals are racing Tesla for first-mover status on European autonomy approvals.
insights.quote: We aim to be one of the first

insights.claim: Five days after the flying Roadster stunt, powered by compressed-gas thrusters from SpaceX, Musk revealed that Tesla and SpaceX were exploring a merger to accelerate autonomous driving.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A merger would restructure Tesla's capital and AI investment capacity.
insights.quote: exploring a merger that could accelerate his push into autonomous driving

insights.claim: The FT frames a merger as giving Tesla firepower against Chinese rivals and Big Tech with far bigger AI budgets, with an integrated company accelerating research in materials, AI and manufacturing while cutting costs and improving access to chips.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Combination is pitched as a way to fund the AI race, but it is untested.
insights.quote: accelerate research into materials, AI, and manufacturing

insights.claim: William Blair's Jed Dorsheimer says the tie-up, if approved by shareholders and regulators, could allow Musk to control 50 percent or more of the merged entity.
insights.speaker: Jed Dorsheimer
insights.so_what: Governance and minority-shareholder concerns rise with greater Musk control.
insights.quote: could allow Musk to control 50 percent or more

insights.claim: One top-15 Tesla shareholder supports the merger, arguing Tesla stands to benefit from all the AI-related innovations now happening at SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: At least some large holders are receptive to the deal.
insights.quote: all the AI-related innovations now happening at SpaceX

insights.claim: Tesla enthusiast Max Willson warns that combining the businesses risks tying their futures to Musk's most speculative bets, so trouble in AI could spread across the group and SpaceX's success should be protected.
insights.speaker: Max Willson
insights.so_what: The merger raises contagion and key-person risk for a currently strong SpaceX.
insights.quote: risks tying their futures to his most speculative bets
insights.locator: But bringing the two businesses together

insights.claim: Tesla is driving wider industry change: Xpeng, Hyundai and Toyota are expanding robotics businesses, while GM and Ford pursue new revenue from energy storage.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Automakers are diversifying into robotics and storage, copying Tesla's playbook.
insights.quote: Tesla is already driving wider change
insights.locator: Whether or not the companies merge

insights.claim: RBC's Tom Narayan calls Tesla a classic case of an innovator that disrupts while the others follow so as not to be left behind.
insights.speaker: Tom Narayan
insights.so_what: Tesla sets the strategic agenda for the industry, even as it loses share.
insights.quote: a classic case of an innovator that disrupts and the other follows

insights.claim: GM hired former Tesla executive Sterling Anderson to oversee product development, with a mandate for a new generation of fully autonomous personal cars; BMW and Mercedes-Benz partner with Qualcomm and Nvidia on Level 2 plus driver assistance that needs active human monitoring.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Legacy OEMs rely on chip and tech partners and Tesla alumni to catch up.
insights.quote: Level 2 plus

insights.claim: Volvo's CEO acknowledges Tesla is probably leading development in the West but claims Volvo is firmly leading in software, and says it will develop door-to-door automated cars with Nvidia pretty soon.
insights.speaker: Håkan Samuelsson
insights.so_what: Even rivals concede Tesla's lead in Western autonomy.
insights.quote: Tesla is probably leading the development in the West
